assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, turned optical frequency standards into a many-atom measurement tool with fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, far beyond the microwave definition of the second. This is the kind of advance in 'what we can measure, and how accurately' that I weigh most heavily: a clear instrument-level breakthrough with direct consequences for relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and a prospective redefinition of the SI second.
assessment.attribution: Katori's 2001-2003 magic-wavelength lattice concept and first demonstration of strontium lattice clocks is the decisive origin. Ye's JILA group brought the clock to record accuracy and stability, together with spin-polarized fermion and many-body clock work. Two laureates give a clean configuration; Hall and Hänsch already took the frequency-comb recognition in 2005, so a separate prize is defensible. Contributions of other lattice-clock groups and ion-clock work (Wineland 2012) are real but do not need inclusion.
assessment.maturity: Independent confirmation across many laboratories (Sr, Yb, Hg) and international comparisons is extensive, and the interpretation is stable. Timing is good, since the redefinition of the second is under active discussion but not complete.
uncertainties: Overlap with the earlier 2005 and 2012 prizes in precision optical metrology may be argued, although the lattice-clock concept is distinct.
Whether Ye or other contributors, such as Hall or Hänsch-adjacent comb developers, should be weighed differently; I rely on general knowledge, not independent verification.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry delivers matter-wave inertial and gravitational sensing of exceptional precision, with measurements of g, G, the fine-structure constant and gravity-gradient tests, and a route to tests of the equivalence principle and gravitational-wave detection concepts. It is a direct realization of precision measurement with laser-cooled atoms, a field I know well.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard's group demonstrated the first atom interferometers with material gratings and light; Bordé's theoretical and Ramsey-Bordé interferometer work gave the optical-pulse framework; Kasevich and Chu realized the light-pulse interferometer with high-precision gravimetry. Three names are credible, but Steven Chu and others who might compete for credit are not in the supplied names, so the allocation is delicate.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with commercial gravimeters and long-baseline instruments, but headline applications such as gravitational-wave detection or equivalence-principle tests at high precision are still developing.
uncertainties: Credit among Pritchard, Bordé, Kasevich and absent contributors such as Chu is contestable.
Whether the field's most important discoveries are yet delivered, as opposed to anticipated, is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection of single nitrogen-vacancy centres and their coherent spin control opened room-temperature solid-state quantum sensing of magnetic fields, temperature and strain at the nanoscale, with biological and materials applications and a path to quantum registers. The combination of single-defect optical readout and long spin coherence is an original and broadly used capability.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko made the decisive single-centre optical detection and coherent control demonstrations; Lukin's group contributed sensing proposals, nuclear-spin registers and many-body applications. A three-person configuration is reasonable, although Lukin's role is more conceptual-and-broad, with other contributors to NV sensing not on the list.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many groups and applied widely, though the sensing portion is still moving quickly toward practical use.
uncertainties: Weighting of Lukin's contributions across other prize candidates, such as Rydberg arrays, is unresolved.
Recognition might favour the early single-defect work over the later sensing applications.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit quantum electrodynamics created strong-coupling light-matter physics on chip and underlies today's superconducting quantum processors: dispersive readout, cavity-mediated gates and quantum-limited amplification chains. Its impact on quantum technology is large and lasting.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Girvin and Schoelkopf produced the 2004 theory and Schoelkopf's and Wallraff's groups the first strong-coupling experiments in the same year. Four names are supplied, which is one too many; I choose Blais, Schoelkopf and Wallraff, but Girvin's contribution is substantial and the choice is not obvious.
assessment.maturity: Replicated worldwide and mature, but the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits has just recognized adjacent superconducting-circuit work, so timing is delicate.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2025 prize and the question whether it leaves less room for circuit work.
Allocation of credit among four principal contributors.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The 1995 Cirac-Zoller proposal for a trapped-ion quantum computer set out a concrete physical architecture, and their work on quantum simulation and quantum networks seeded much of experimental quantum information. The clarity and influence of the proposal are very high.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller are clearly the two decisive contributors; a two-person configuration is clean. The experimental ion-trap work is credited elsewhere, and Wineland was already honoured in 2012.
assessment.maturity: Experiments in ion traps and neutral atoms have repeatedly confirmed the architecture, but the full promise of scalable quantum computing is unproven, so the timing is arguably mixed.
uncertainties: Whether a theory-led prize is preferred to experimental breakthroughs.
Overlap with candidate B006, which names the same two people.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Titanium-sapphire gain media and Kerr-lens/passive mode-locking made reliable femtosecond lasers routine and enabled frequency combs, ultrafast spectroscopy and much more. As a laser tool its importance is enormous, though some recognition already exists in 1999 and 2018 prizes on femtochemistry and chirped-pulse amplification.
assessment.attribution: Moulton invented the Ti:sapphire laser; Sibbett's group demonstrated Kerr-lens mode locking; Keller developed semiconductor saturable absorber mirrors for passive mode-locking. Attribution is plausible but spans different inventions, so a three-person prize would be a compound arrangement.
assessment.maturity: Very mature and long confirmed, so it is timely or even late.
uncertainties: Whether Kerr-lens mode locking (Sibbett and colleagues) and SESAM mode locking (Keller) are one discovery or two.
Potential overlap with earlier ultrafast-laser prizes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: BB84 and E91 established quantum key distribution with security rooted in quantum mechanics, and the protocols are realized in fibre and satellite links. The conceptual originality is high and the impact on quantum information science is lasting.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard authored BB84; Ekert's 1991 entanglement-based protocol is a distinct contribution. A three-person prize is plausible, although Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea and recognition of entanglement in 2022 complicate credit.
assessment.maturity: Mature in principle; practical deployment and security against implementation attacks are still developing.
uncertainties: Prior recognition of entanglement experiments in 2022 may reduce the margin.
Wiesner's role and possible overlap with other QKD pioneers.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation of Hubbard models with ultracold atoms in optical lattices, including the superfluid to Mott insulator transition and quantum gas microscopes, gives controllable many-body systems that probe problems in condensed matter. The conceptual and experimental importance is high.
assessment.attribution: Bloch and Greiner carried out the decisive experimental demonstrations and microscopy; the theoretical proposal of Jaksch, Zoller, Cirac and colleagues is also essential, so I select the experimentalists, but the allocation of theory credit is unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed and widely replicated, though bosonic condensation and cooling were previously recognized, and quantitative advantage over classical computation in fermionic Hubbard regimes is still developing.
uncertainties: Theory versus experiment credit allocation, including the role of Cirac and Zoller.
Overlap with earlier BEC and cooling prizes.
